name: 3 John
subtitle: A Friendship Made of Scripture
howToRead: The most personal letter in the New Testament commends Gaius for walking in the truth and welcoming traveling brothers, rebukes Diotrephes who loves to be first and turns them away, and bears witness to Demetrius. Its closing is unique in the canon — the friends greet you; greet the friends by name. Beneath the small drama of hospitality lies the old scriptural law of welcoming the stranger and imitating good rather than evil. The chips beside each passage name the Scripture underneath it — solid for a formal quotation, dashed for an allusion, dotted for a fainter echo, ◇ for a figural pattern that borrows no words. A lighter chip and a trailing ? mark an echo that is faint or contested. Where the writer follows the Greek of the Septuagint against the Hebrew, both readings are shown.

pericopes.text: The elder to Gaius the beloved, whom I love in truth. Beloved, I pray that you may prosper in all things and be healthy, even as your soul prospers. For I rejoiced greatly, when brothers came and testified about your truth, even as you walk in truth. I have no greater joy than this, to hear about my children walking in truth.

echoes.text: Teach me your way, Yahweh. I will walk in your truth. Make my heart undivided to fear your name.
echoes.note: The letter's keynote, Gaius and the elder's children 'walking in truth,' draws on the Psalter's idiom for fidelity to God's revealed way: 'teach me your way, O LORD; I will walk in your truth.' The same construction of walking in/according to truth recurs as the praise the elder repeats four times.

echoes.text: That Yahweh may establish his word which he spoke concerning me, saying, ‘If your children take heed to their way, to walk before me in truth with all their heart and with all their soul, there shall not fail you,’ he said, ‘a man on the throne of Israel.’
echoes.note: The Deuteronomistic standard for the faithful, who 'walk before me in truth with all their heart,' supplies the covenantal background for the elder's joy that his children walk in truth. Cf. also 2 Kings 20:3.

echoes.text: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.
echoes.note: The prayer that Gaius 'may prosper in all things' as his soul prospers loosely recalls the wisdom promise that the righteous one 'in whatever he does, he prospers.' The link is thematic rather than verbal and the everyday health-wish formula carries most of the freight.

pericopes.text: Beloved, you do a faithful work in whatever you accomplish for those who are brothers and strangers. They have testified about your love before the assembly. You will do well to send them forward on their journey in a way worthy of God, because for the sake of the Name they went out, taking nothing from the Gentiles. We therefore ought to receive such, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]
echoes.note: Gaius's reception of brothers who are also 'strangers' and his sending them on worthily reflects the patriarchal paradigm of hospitality, where Abraham receives unknown travelers and provisions them for the road. This Abrahamic model stands behind the early Christian valuing of welcome to itinerant messengers.

echoes.text: The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: The praise of love shown to 'brothers and strangers' rests on the Holiness Code's command that the sojourner be treated as a native and loved as oneself. The pairing of love and the resident alien gives the commendation its scriptural weight.

echoes.text: Therefore love the foreigner; for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic charge to 'love the stranger' undergirds the elder's commendation of hospitality to traveling brothers who are strangers to Gaius. It belongs to the same Torah tradition of sheltering the sojourner that the letter assumes as virtue.

pericopes.text: I wrote to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, doesn’t accept what we say. Therefore if I come, I will call attention to his deeds which he does, unjustly accusing us with wicked words. Not content with this, neither does he himself receive the brothers, and those who would, he forbids and throws out of the assembly.

echoes.text: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.
echoes.note: Diotrephes 'who loves to be first' and lords it over the assembly embodies the proud heart that wisdom warns precedes destruction. The portrait of self-exaltation refusing the brothers is drawn against the Proverbs critique of haughtiness.

echoes.text: An unfriendly man pursues selfishness, and defies all sound judgment.
echoes.note: Diotrephes, who isolates the church from the elder's emissaries and expels those who would receive them, recalls the wisdom saying about one who separates himself and rejects sound counsel. The connection is thematic.

echoes.text: He who hides hatred has lying lips. He who utters a slander is a fool.
echoes.note: His 'unjustly accusing us with wicked words' resonates with the wisdom condemnation of the slanderer and the one who utters falsehood. A faint sapiential coloring rather than a specific citation.

pericopes.text: Beloved, don’t imitate that which is evil, but that which is good. He who does good is of God. He who does evil hasn’t seen God.

echoes.text: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.
echoes.note: The exhortation 'don't imitate that which is evil, but that which is good' restates the psalm's classic two-ways summons to 'depart from evil, and do good.' The antithesis of evil and good as a moral test of belonging to God is the same.

echoes.text: Depart from evil, and do good. Live securely forever.
echoes.note: 'Depart from evil, and do good; and dwell forevermore' parallels the letter's contrast between the one who does good and is of God and the one who does evil and has not seen God. The reward of abiding maps onto the Johannine sense of being 'of God.'

echoes.text: Wash yourselves, make yourself clean. Put away the evil of your doings from before my eyes. Cease to do evil. Learn to do well. Seek justice. Relieve the oppressed. Judge the fatherless. Plead for the widow.”
echoes.note: The prophetic call to 'cease to do evil; learn to do well' supplies the same evil/good imperative that the elder applies to discerning true discipleship. One strand of the broader scriptural two-ways tradition.

echoes.text: Seek good, and not evil, that you may live; and so Yahweh, the God of Armies, will be with you, as you say. Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the courts. It may be that Yahweh, the God of Armies, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.”
echoes.note: 'Seek good, and not evil, that you may live... Hate evil, love good' shares the moral logic that doing good aligns one with God and doing evil estranges one from him. A thematic echo within the prophetic two-ways material.

pericopes.text: Demetrius has the testimony of all, and of the truth itself; yes, we also testify, and you know that our testimony is true.

echoes.text: A good name is more desirable than great riches, and loving favor is better than silver and gold.
echoes.note: Demetrius 'has the testimony of all, and of the truth itself' commends the good name that wisdom prizes above riches: 'a good name is rather to be chosen than great riches.' The value placed on public good repute stands behind the commendation.

echoes.text: A good name is better than fine perfume; and the day of death better than the day of one’s birth.
echoes.note: The well-attested name of Demetrius faintly recalls Qoheleth's praise that 'a good name is better than precious ointment.' A general sapiential valuing of reputation rather than a deliberate citation.

pericopes.text: I had many things to write to you, but I am unwilling to write to you with ink and pen; but I hope to see you soon, and we will speak face to face. Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends by name.

echoes.text: Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The closing benediction 'Peace be to you' carries the priestly blessing's gift of shalom, the customary Hebrew word of farewell and blessing. The link is to a standard liturgical formula rather than a pointed allusion.
